# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

</document>
response:
This is a strong follow-up. It resolves several open questions directly: it adds a second hours measure, registers the mediation test, publishes the decay comparison, and reports that the counter arm was ended. It also answers the meta-analysis's duration claim convincingly. Its weaknesses are mostly in presentation and in interpreting a few results. The Summary overstates the decline, the meetings result is stated as more certain than it is, and the control offices' meeting audit is treated as a curiosity when it actually biases the 24-month comparison.

## Arithmetic check

| Item | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| Per hour, timesheets | 0.966 / 0.88 = 1.098 | +9.8% ✓ |
| Per hour, logs | 0.966 / 0.89 = 1.085 | +8.5% ✓ |
| CIs | Output CI ÷ hours ratio ≈ +4.5 to +15.0 and +3.4 to +13.7 | ✓ (close) |
| Mediation shares | 47 + 18 + 35 = 100 | ✓ |
| Halden 11 | 34.9 / 40.3 = 0.866; 96.8 / 86.6 = 1.118 | +11.8% ✓ |
| Counter staffing | Restoring output lost at −11.4% needs 1 / 0.886 ≈ 13% more staff | 12% ✓ |
| **Counter cost** | 12% more staff at the same pay → +12% labour cost per contact vs control | **9% unexplained** |
| **Control meetings** | Two control offices fell by 2.1 h each, yet the control mean fell only 0.2 h | **Implies the other five *rose* about 0.5 h each** |

The 9% cost figure is plausible if it counts total costs (non-staff overheads dilute the 12% staff increase), but the basis should be stated. The meetings figures can't all be right unless the other control offices increased their meeting time. That would be worth confirming, and reporting if true.

## Main problems

**1. The Summary compares two different measures to describe the decline.**
"Fell from 12.5% … to 8.5%, measured with system log data" sets a timesheet figure (12.5%) against a log figure (8.5%). The like-for-like comparison is 12.5% → 9.8%. That is a fall of about a fifth, not a third. Section 5's "about a quarter" matches neither comparison.
The decline is also not tested. The two intervals (6.9–18.4 and 4.6–15.2) overlap heavily. Because the offices are the same, a direct test of the difference is possible and should be reported. Until then, "the gain has declined" should read "the point estimate is lower."

**2. The control-office meeting audit contaminates the 24-month comparison.**
At month 15, two of the seven control offices cut meetings and gained about 4.1% output per hour. This affects the results in two ways:
- **It lowers the treatment effect.** If the two offices are of similar size, control productivity rose by roughly 1 percentage point. Part of the apparent fall from 12.5% to 9.8% may therefore come from the control group improving, not from the treatment effect fading.
- **It weakens the mediation contrast.** The difference in meeting time between arms shrinks. This would bias the estimated meetings share in a direction that depends on the model.

The authors should report the main estimates and the mediation analysis with and without these two offices, or adjusted for the audit. As it stands, the observation sits in the paper as an aside when it bears directly on Table 1.

**3. It is unclear what the log-hours measure captures.**
Active log-in time on the case-management system may leave out meetings, email and phone work. That matters in two ways:
- **If logs exclude meetings:** they cannot be a stricter version of timesheet hours. Using the paper's own numbers, non-meeting time fell by only about 4–5% (treated ≈ 33.4 − 3.9 h; control ≈ 37.9 − 7.0 h). Logs that excluded meetings should show roughly that fall, not −11%. And if output per *log* hour is the mediation outcome, cutting meetings would barely move its denominator. Any mediated effect would then have to work through fewer interruptions, not reallocated time. That is a different mechanism from the one the text describes.
- **If logs include meetings:** the description ("time staff are working on cases") needs correcting.

There is also the question of baselines. Logs were "added" at follow-up and no nine-month log figure is given. Yet the difference-in-differences needs pre-period log hours. Were these retrieved after the fact? If so, why is there no nine-month log estimate?

**4. The mediation result is stated with more certainty than the design supports.**
- **"Confirms" is too strong.** The Summary says the registered test "confirms" the meetings pathway, but mediation depends on an assumption a cluster trial cannot check: no unmeasured confounding between mediator and outcome. The Limitations section admits this; the Summary should match it. The meeting cuts were not randomised. Managers who cut meetings may also have made other improvements.
- **The effective sample is small.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds repeated measurements, not independent units. The effective sample is still 14 offices. With a total effect of 8.5% (3.4–13.8), a share-mediated interval as narrow as 28–66% looks optimistic. The authors should state the inference method; a cluster bootstrap would be appropriate.
- **It is not an independent replication.** The registered test uses the same seven treated offices that generated the exploratory hypothesis. Registration at month 11 protects the later outcome data, not the choice of offices.
- **The shares may not add up.** Meetings and fatigue may interact; fewer meetings could itself reduce fatigue. The authors should say whether the shares come from a joint model and whether they can legitimately be summed.

**5. The Halden reversions are summarised too loosely.**
The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a marketing agency citing client deadlines. That is discretionary work under deadline pressure, not coverage-bound work. Grouping it with retail and hospitality makes the reversions look neater than they are. More precisely: two of three reversions were coverage-bound, and one was a discretionary firm that could not meet deadlines. That third case is a relevant failure for the discretionary story.

Three smaller points on this section:
- **Non-response:** 9 of the 23 organisations didn't respond, which adds a third layer of selection on top of the two the paper notes.
- **"Upper bound" is too strong:** an uncontrolled estimate is likely biased upward, but it isn't strictly a bound. General economic conditions could push it either way.
- **Baseline hours:** the baseline of 40.3 matches the 27-organisation figure from the re-analysis exactly, while the 17-organisation subset was 40.4. This may be coincidence, but it is worth confirming that the correct subset's baseline was used.

## Smaller points

- **Few-cluster inference is still unaddressed.** With seven offices per arm, "excludes zero by a clear margin" depends on how the CIs were computed. A wild cluster bootstrap or randomisation inference would settle this. It is the same open question as at nine months.
- **Conflict of interest.** A Halden author co-writes the Halden follow-up, and the Varden authors are testing their own hypothesis against critics. That is normal, but the wording of the Summary ("confirms," "all client-facing") leans in their favour in exactly the places where it overstates.
- **Section 5 on the re-analysis is fair.** The 24-month Varden estimate does meet the standards Varga and Holm set out, and the rebuttal credits their valid points.
- **Section 5 on the meta-analysis is decisive.** It shows that all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. That confirms the "no decay" conclusion was a design artifact.

## How this updates the overall picture

| Question | Before | After this report |
|---|---|---|
| Per-hour gain, discretionary work, rigorous design | ~10–12% at 9 months | ~8.5–10% at 24 months; still clearly above zero |
| Decay | Unknown | Point estimate down ~20% like-for-like; not tested; partly confounded by control contamination |
| Coverage-bound work | Output per worker −9 to −11% | Confirmed and costly; arm ended; ~12% more staff needed |
| Meetings mechanism | Exploratory | Supported by a registered test, but relies on untestable mediation assumptions; about half the gain |
| Gain without cutting hours? | Untested | Suggestive two-office observation; needs a reorganisation-only arm |

The most useful next study would be the one this report identifies but cannot run: an arm that reorganises meetings without cutting hours. That is the only way to tell whether the shorter week causes the gain or merely forces changes that could happen anyway.

I can draft a referee report, or update the cross-paper evidence summary to include this follow-up, if useful.
